message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc.). | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of any needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or seek a court order. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are limited to **$25** per month (unless the lease says otherwise). | • Keep receipts or bank records.
• If you’re late, notify the landlord and negotiate a payment plan. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord may only terminate for cause (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease). | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail).
• Keep a copy of the notice. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice of entry.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint or seek damages. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may **deduct the cost** from your rent (up to the amount of the repair) and pay the landlord the remainder. | • Keep receipts and provide the landlord with a written notice of the deduction. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must serve a **30‑day notice** for non‑payment or a **60‑day notice** for lease violations.
• If the landlord files an eviction lawsuit, you have the right to contest it in court. | • Respond to the notice promptly.
• Attend the court hearing and bring evidence (e.g., proof of rent payment, repair requests). | | **Rent Control & Rent Increase** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control laws. Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | • Review the lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the service. | • Keep utility bills and communicate any outages. | | **Insurance** | • Tenants are not required to carry renters’ insurance, but it’s highly recommended to protect personal property. | • Purchase a policy covering theft, fire, water damage, etc. | | **Legal Assistance** | • If you face eviction or other disputes, you can seek help from:
• Texas Legal Services (for low‑income tenants).
• Local tenant‑rights groups.
• Pro bono attorneys. | • Contact the organization, provide documentation, and follow their guidance. | #### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – note rent amount, due date, security deposit, pet policy, maintenance responsibilities, and notice periods. 2. **Document the condition** – take photos or videos of the unit and keep a copy of the move‑in inspection report. 3. **Ask for a written copy of the lease** – keep it in a safe place. 4. **Know your local ordinances** – some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections. #### When Things Go Wrong - **Non‑payment of rent**: Send a written notice of intent to pay and ask for a payment plan. - **Unresolved repairs**: File a written complaint with the landlord, then with TDHCA if unresolved. - **Unlawful eviction notice**: File a complaint with TCHR or HUD, and consult an attorney. --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, fair notice before entry, protection against discrimination, and a clear process for ending a lease or contesting an eviction. Keep all communications in writing, document everything, and know where to seek help if needed.
